name: PT Sumber Alfaria Trijaya Tbk

frontmatter.title: Alfamart: a growth franchise priced for a store cap that does not yet exist
frontmatter.summary: The 10 November press report restates the nine-month revenue and attributable profit already in the 30 September accounts and adds one comparison: Midi, the group's convenience format, grew profit several times faster on a fresh-food mix. It brings no new period or operating number, so the rating and target stand; the forecast carries two corrections from the LK's own rates and share count.
thesis: The 10 November recap puts nine-month revenue at IDR101,000.0bn and net profit at IDR2,400.0bn, which is the attributable line of IDR2,402.8bn up 3.8% — figures the September accounts already carry [S12][S3].

Expansion has not stopped: 1,081 net new Alfamart stores in 2025 and a 800 target for 2026, against a ministerial statement about new permits only and one regency enforcing a rule in force since 2021.
Last-actual economics are stable: gross margin held at 21.9% through FY2025 and the first nine months of FY2026, operating margin 3.6% on the restated basis.
The de-rating did the damage, not the earnings: 12.0x forward earnings and 4.2x EV/EBITDA against a five-year average in the high twenties.
Net cash, negative working capital and a 50.0% payout support a 4.2% yield while the growth is re-priced; IDR532.8bn of shares were bought back in the nine months to September [S3].
Base-case intrinsic value Rp1,351 a share, probability-weighted twelve-month target Rp1,530; the bear case's twelve-month value is Rp544, roughly half today's price, and is the honest downside.

catalysts.event: FY2026 audited results: fourth-quarter revenue and the full-year net operating-expense ratio
FY2027 expansion plan published with the annual report
Annual general meeting: FY2026 final dividend and payout policy
Vietnam entry: first stores if the local partner is signed

blocks.text: **BUY, target Rp1,530 (61.1% total return), base-case intrinsic value Rp1,351 against a share price of Rp975.** The 10 November report brings no new period and no new operating number [S12]: its nine-month revenue IDR101,000.0bn and profit IDR2,400.0bn restate the 30 September accounts [S12][S3]. The profit figure is the attributable line of IDR2,402.8bn, not the IDR2,558.9bn total including minorities, so profit grew at roughly half the operating rate [S3]. The rating and target stand, but the model moved: FY2026E attributable profit is now IDR3,342.7bn on restated finance cost and non-operating items, and the share count carries the IDR532.8bn buyback [S3].

The report adds one genuine piece of analysis, and it is not flattering: Midi grew nine-month net profit 19.4% against 3.8% at Alfamart, on the ready-to-eat and ready-to-drink mix of the Lawson format [S12]. It is a format question, not evidence that Alfamart's grocery margin is being lost, but it is a real signal and stays in the bear case. The rest — a stable staple basket, additions beyond Java, a year-end push, a cost warning on logistics and food inflation — is the environment we already model [S12].
What changed is the story, not the operating record: the February permit call, narrowed to new permits only, one regency closing outlets under a 2021 rule, and the MSCI exit [S7][S11][S8].

Our variant view is narrow. A national cap on new stores is the most damaging thing that could happen to this model and it is the bear case; the evidence so far is rhetoric plus local enforcement of pre-existing rules, while the plan and nine-month revenue assume expansion continues [S5][S3]. No source says the state wants the chains to supply the cooperatives: they are a subsidised rural competitor, not a distribution channel [S7]. Three judgements carry the thesis: the store programme runs at the guided pace, gross margin holds, and the DCF is the right valuation.

Sumber Alfaria Trijaya runs the Alfamart minimarket chain and adjacent retail formats in Indonesia [S6]. At end-FY2025 it operated 24,434 outlets, of which 21,120 trade under the Alfamart banner, with 175,177 employees [S6]. It added 1,081 net new Alfamart stores in 2025 and guided to 800 net additions in 2026, concentrated outside the Jakarta suburbs [S5]; the November article describes the same programme as measured but aggressive beyond Java [S12].

The mix is food with a non-food tail: food produced IDR72,140.0bn of nine-month revenue against IDR29,140.0bn from non-food, so food is gaining share [S9] — it carries the traffic and the supplier funding, non-food the ticket. Operating profit also carries recurring other operating income of IDR1,333.7bn in FY2025 — payment fees, space rental, franchise administration, registration — which we treat as operating, earned every year of the record [S4].

The model is cash-generative in a way that is easy to miss: suppliers fund the shelf, so operating working capital is negative and growth releases cash [S0]. Most stores are leased: right-of-use depreciation of IDR2,492.1bn exceeds owned fixed-asset depreciation of IDR1,786.3bn [S4].

Abroad, Alfamart runs in the Philippines through a 35.0% associate with 2,700 stores, plus a small Bangladesh presence and a Vietnam entry guided for late 2026 or early 2027 [S10][S4]. Equity-accounted, so none of its earnings are in our cash flow; its carrying value of IDR348.7bn sits in the valuation bridge [S4].

Control sits with PT Sigmantara Alfindo at 50.2%, the founding family behind it and on the board [S6]. Alfagift, the loyalty and ordering platform, had 29 million members at end-2025 [S5]. Strategy is store expansion, supply-chain optimisation, then digital [S6].

Indonesian minimarket retail is a duopoly — Alfamart and Indomaret national, a long tail below [S2]. The leaders compete store by store on location, hours and promotion, and buy from the same manufacturers, so gross margins converge [S2]. The question is how much format is left and how much value the state reallocates.

That question became live in 2026. The Minister of Villages argued new minimarket permits should stop so village cooperatives are not undercut, then clarified he meant new permits, not closures [S7]. The same report builds Koperasi Desa Merah Putih as the backbone of the village economy and judges the chains to create unbalanced competition [S7] — the opposite of the chain-as-distributor reading, since the cooperative is a subsidised rural competitor and the instrument against it is licensing. Permits are issued by regencies, so the instrument is blunt: Lombok Tengah applied its own distance rule and the operators closed the offending outlets [S11].

Competition inside the group is the more informative signal. Midi grew nine-month net profit 19.4% against 3.8% at Alfamart, on margin and operating efficiency and specifically the ready-to-eat and ready-to-drink mix of the Lawson format, a higher-margin mix than regular groceries [S12]. That is consistent with our flat gross margin: Alfamart's 21.9% is a grocery mix funded by supplier terms, and we assume no move in it, so we are not capitalising the margin Midi is earning. It does bear on the bear case, where a format that cannot add fresh-food margin competes on price and location — the path in which a hundred basis points of gross margin go to promotion. It also explains why group profit growth is shared below the operating line [S3].

The moat is distribution density: warehouses and branch offices that double as depots place a case of water at a village outlet at a landed cost an independent shop cannot match, while holding almost no inventory because suppliers own stock until it is scanned [S6]. Durable against entrants, weak against location rules. Supplier power low, buyer power moderate, entry threat low, substitutes moderate, rivalry high [S2].

Demand is the constraint nobody can legislate away. Purchasing power is weak and the listed retail names reporting in November described trade-down [S2], yet revenue reached IDR101,288.2bn in the first nine months, ahead of last year [S3], and the 10 November article says the same qualitatively [S12]. For a format selling rice, oil and soap, weak real income compresses basket size, not visit frequency [S2]. Regulation cuts both ways: medicines sales are now allowed, a higher-margin adjacency [S6].

Revenue compounded from IDR96,924.7bn in FY2022 to IDR126,737.3bn in FY2025, decelerating to 7.2% as the base matured [S4]. The nine months to September reached IDR101,288.2bn, ahead of last year, so deceleration stopped [S3]; the November restatement to IDR101,000.0bn is the same number seen from outside [S12]. We model 7.2% for FY2026E, then 7.0% fading to 6.1%: 800 net new stores on 21,120 banner outlets is roughly three per cent of the estate before like-for-like, and the fade is arithmetic [S5][S9]. No source caps the programme.

Gross margin has been flat: 21.5% in FY2024, 21.9% in FY2025 and unchanged in the nine months of FY2026 [S4][S3], and we hold 21.9%. Mix shifts toward food, marginally higher-margin on supplier funding, but promotion caps the upside.

The operating-expense line decides the argument, and needs care because other operating income sits above it. Net of that income the ratio was lower in FY2025 than in the first nine months of FY2026, as wages and ramp costs bit [S4][S3]. We hold 18.6%, the nine-month actual blended with the fourth quarter's seasonally lower ratio rather than extrapolating the creep for a decade; the blend leaves the full-year margin lower than FY2025's and makes the calibration gap auditable [S3][S4]. With gross margin at 21.9%, operating margin is a shade below FY2025 [S3]; the error sits in the bear case, where the ratio rises half a point.

Operating margin is 3.6% in FY2025 and 3.3% in FY2026E, EBITDA IDR9,063.7bn growing to IDR9,279.4bn [S4]. Right-of-use depreciation alone was IDR2,492.1bn, which is why EBITDA flatters this business and why we value free cash flow after capex of IDR4,994.7bn, held near that share of revenue [S4].

Below the operating line the year is not a repeat of FY2025, and the model says so on the accounts' own rates. Finance cost was IDR127.2bn in the nine months, annualising to about the IDR169.7bn we carry against IDR137.3bn in FY2025 [S3][S4]; that charge covers bank and lease interest at the LK's rate, not the 9.4% marginal rate used in the cost of capital. Other non-operating items are held at IDR-81.0bn, the nine-month run rate annualised, rather than FY2025's heavier associate loss [S3][S4].

The earnings path follows: nine-month earnings per share of Rp58, a full-year Rp81 against Rp82 [S3]. Attributable profit of IDR3,342.7bn is a little below FY2025's IDR3,410.9bn on revenue growth of 7.2%, because the operating-expense ratio is 18.6% against IDR23,193.9bn of cost on IDR126,737.3bn of revenue, and the minority take is 6.1% against about four per cent [S3][S4].

Cash conversion is the strongest part of the record: operating cash flow exceeds net profit every year, negative working capital makes growth self-funding, and September carried more cash than debt [S0][S4]. Trade receivables are the place to look: a IDR3,214.3bn book owed for rent, promotion and franchise settlement rather than by shoppers, of which IDR12.9bn — under half a per cent — is related parties, with about 53.6% not yet due [S4].

Capital allocation suits a business needing no external capital. Policy obliges a payout above a quarter of profit and practice is closer to half: FY2025 was distributed at Rp42 a share, IDR1,705.3bn of it paid in the first nine months of FY2026 against FY2025 attributable profit of IDR3,410.9bn [S3][S6]. Our Rp41 is the assumed payout on FY2026E. The company also bought back IDR532.8bn of shares in the nine months, raising treasury shares to 432.7 million, so FY2026E earnings per share are struck on the smaller base [S3]. The programme ran to a March 2026 expiry with no renewal on file, so we assume no further buyback. Cash is accumulating that the business does not need — IDR5,438.5bn against IDR2,710.4bn of debt — a mild valuation drag.

Earnings quality on the house screen: accruals negative, cash conversion stable, no development-cost creep, unqualified FY2025 opinion from an Ernst & Young member firm [S4]. The IDX structure flags — serial rights issues, pledged control, auditor down-tiering — are absent. The related-party channel is disclosed and small [S4][S6]. One question stays open: capital injected into an affiliate-controlled international holding vehicle, terms unsourced, so we flag rather than model it.

We value AMRT on free cash flow to the firm over ten years with terminal value at nine tenths weight, plus the same cash flows without terminal value at one tenth. The multiples are unusable: the stock's own five-year averages were set in the premium era the shares have given back, and capitalising today's profit at yesterday's premium manufactures a target from the very de-rating we are assessing. The declared peers — MIDI, ERAA, MAPI — include one modelled name, below the three for a median, so they get no weight. The no-terminal-value case is the cross-check.

The cost of capital is built from the house deck: a rupiah risk-free rate of 7.4%, less the sovereign spread, plus a levered beta of 0.73 on an equity risk premium of 4.2% plus a country risk premium of 2.5%, and 0.8% for single-format concentration and thin post-index liquidity [S8]. That gives cost of equity 11.5% and, with debt at 4.7% of capital at 9.4% pre-tax, WACC 11.3%. Terminal growth of 5.0% is the house cap.

The DCF gives enterprise value of IDR58,382.4bn and Rp1,433 a share, with terminal value 57.7% of the total. The same cash flows without terminal value are worth Rp614; weighted 90.0% and 10.0%, the two anchors give the base value of Rp1,351, from which the scenarios and target are built. The no-terminal-value leg is -57.2% against the primary, the engine flags it, and it measures how much of the value sits after the explicit forecast.

Growth is manufactured, not declared. In FY2025 capex of IDR4,994.7bn against D&A of IDR4,501.3bn is net reinvestment of roughly an eighth of post-tax operating profit against revenue growth of 7.2% — incremental returns around four times the cost of capital, because suppliers fund the shelf. That excess return fades: return on equity falls from 19.8% to 15.0%, still above the 11.5% cost of equity. The moat earning the residual is distribution density [S6]; a full fade would lower the value.

The survival test. At Rp975 the equity is 12.0x FY2026E earnings and 4.2x EV/EBITDA; at Rp1,351 those earnings are capitalised about a third higher, and terminal value implies an exit multiple about a third above entry. Both are on one definition — market capitalisation net of treasury shares, plus net debt, plus minority interest — so entry and implied exit are like for like, the exit being gross of the minority. The DCF therefore assumes a re-rating; what we claim is narrower: 4.2x EBITDA and 12.0x earnings is a de-rated price for a net-cash franchise earning 19.8% on equity and still building stores. Of the 61.1% return, the cash-flow part is the 4.2% yield plus FY2027E growth of 7.7% — roughly the cost of equity; the rest is re-rating, and a holder who never gets it earns his cost of equity and no more.

Across a two-point spread in cost of capital and terminal growth every sensitivity cell remains above today's price, so the call survives the WACC a full point higher and terminal growth a point lower. It depends on the programme not being legislated away and the multiple not staying de-rated for ever.

At Rp975 the market capitalises IDR40,064.5bn of equity, 12.0x earnings, 4.2x EV/EBITDA and a 4.2% yield, for net cash and return on equity around 19.8% [S0][S4]. The reverse DCF solves to FY2027E growth of 2.3%, against our 7.0% and the 7.2% running now [S3]: the price already assumes the programme stalls.

The regulatory risk matters most. A national stop on new permits would close nothing but remove the growth engine, leaving same-store growth at inflation — roughly the bear case. Likelihood is low near term because licensing sits with regencies and the ministers retreated from closure; impact is severe [S7]. Local enforcement is likelier and less damaging, and a subsidised village-cooperative programme is its longer-term form [S7]; Lombok cost a batch of outlets out of tens of thousands [S11].

Purchasing power is the second risk and is in the numbers: real incomes are squeezed and staples are not immune to smaller baskets [S2]; the November article adds logistics and food inflation squeezing margin [S12]. The bear case carries that path rather than the permit story: growth down three points, the model's shock bound, to below CPI, for a twelve-month value of Rp544. We do not stack the shocks: a weak consumer is the political condition in which the rhetoric hardens.

The below-the-line channel is visible: operating profit grows faster than net profit as the minority take rises to 6.1% [S3], and we hold that ratio, which costs earnings per share and dividends. The receivable book is much smaller: about 53.6% of the IDR3,214.3bn book was current at the FY2025 year end and related parties are IDR12.9bn of it [S4].

Cost inflation is deliberately out of the base case. Minimum wages rise every year and a store opened in the second half carries a full cost base against partial revenue; if the operating-expense ratio creeps half a point a year, operating margin compresses from the mid-threes to the low twos — the bear case, and the assumption most likely to hurt.

The value trap is the fourth the red team forced. At an unchanged 4.2x multiple the twelve-month return is the 4.2% yield plus growth of 7.7% — roughly the cost of equity — and nothing else. A name deleted from the MSCI index can trade de-rated for years while the business compounds [S8]. We give the discount closing within a year no more than even odds; the target is a value roll, not a dated event.

Governance and liquidity complete the list: no pledge of the controlling stake, a top-tier auditor with an unqualified opinion, a consistent dividend record [S6][S4], and IDR63.8bn of three-month turnover with the passive bid gone [S8]. The house macro stance argues for care with leveraged, rate-sensitive consumer names, and AMRT is neither — net cash, rupiah earn and spend, imported content a minority of the basket. To be wrong on the sector AVOID, weak incomes must persist through FY2027 and the rhetoric become national regulation.

The scenarios are mirrored on the same four drivers — revenue growth, gross margin, the operating-expense ratio and terminal growth — at 30.0% bear, 45.0% base and 25.0% bull, with the twelve-month and intrinsic values in the table. Bear lands a demand recession and the permit cap together; bull has demand recovering, rules clarified and the programme running past forecast.

The weights are the weakest input, so we test them. Hold the values fixed and double the bear weight while dropping the bull: the weighted target falls below today's price, so the BUY depends on a base case we judge more likely than not, not on the bull tail. The bull, at 25.0%, supplies close to half the target, the honest way to read Rp1,530. We keep 30.0% bear because it needs a demand recession and a national permit cap at once, and licensing sits with regencies [S7][S11]; we keep the bull because it needs the rules settled and purchasing power recovered in the same window. A second regency enforcing closures at scale would raise the bear weight, not the bear value.

Signposts: a national regulation restricting new permits that survives a legal challenge; a second and third regency following Lombok with enforced closures at scale; a full-year operating-expense ratio above the nine-month run-rate without a revenue offset; any evidence the programme is being cut by the company rather than the state. A ministerial statement that the regime is settled, or Vietnam closing on schedule, would remove the overhang faster than the accounts [S10][S7].

Ownership is concentrated and stable: PT Sigmantara Alfindo holds 50.2%, the founding family behind it and on the board [S6]; the standard IDX question is whether growth is funded at the listed company or diverted to affiliates. Related-party flows are disclosed — franchise and service fees, a IDR3,214.3bn trade-receivables book of which IDR12.9bn is related parties, and a Philippines associate whose carrying value has fallen with its losses [S4][S6] — and none distorts the consolidated margin.

The audit is clean: unqualified opinion from an Ernst & Young member firm on FY2025, no emphasis of matter [S4]. Dividends have risen every year, now semi-annual with an October 2026 interim [S6][S9]. No pledge, no rights issue, no auditor change; the board is family-weighted with independent commissioners and an audit committee [S6].

ESG exposures are those of the format. Packaging waste across tens of thousands of stores is the visible environmental issue, with a reported reduction programme [S6]. Labour is the material social issue: a large store workforce in a country where minimum wages are set annually and politically, which is why the wage line is both an ESG and a profit line.

The near-term catalysts are operational. The FY2026 report shows whether the fourth quarter kept the revenue rate and whether the operating-expense ratio ended at or below the nine-month level; that line decides between base and bear [S3]. The FY2027 plan tests whether the rhetoric changed company behaviour [S5]. The AGM sets the final dividend, which at this price matters as much as earnings [S6].

The regulatory calendar is less predictable and more valuable: any ministerial or regency rule on location, zoning or hours would move the shares more than a quarter of earnings, as would a second regency enforcing closures [S11]. We also watch the medicines rollout and Vietnam [S10].

Between reports we monitor four KPIs: net store additions against guidance, revenue growth split between new stores and like-for-like, the operating-expense ratio, and dividend per share. A fifth is the tone of the cooperative programme [S7]. The 10 November recap changed none of them [S12].

valuation.label: DCF to end of life (no terminal value)

bear.narrative: A domestic demand recession lands on top of the permit dispute: real incomes fall, shoppers trade down to the traditional shop and the cooperative, revenue growth loses three points (the model's shock bound, from 7.2% to about 4% and below CPI, so real same-store sales turn negative), price competition takes 100bp of gross margin, minimum-wage and new-store ramp costs add 50bp to the opex ratio, and the mature network grows at 4.0%. The receivable and minority channels are stated rather than shocked: the aging table shows the book slowing, and a 6.1% minority take is a permanent leak on subsidiary-led growth.

bull.narrative: Clearer national rules settle the radius disputes and household purchasing power recovers, so the 800-store-a-year programme runs past 2027 and same-store sales beat CPI by three points as the Alfagift base lifts basket size; mix and scale add 100bp of gross margin, the opex ratio falls 50bp and the mature network grows at 6.0%.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

football.label: DCF to end of life (no terminal value)

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: Revenue = net store additions x sales per store. FY2026E 7.2% is the 9M2026 actual (S3); the 800-store 2026 plan on 21,120 Alfamart banner outlets is 3.8% unit growth (S5, S6) and CPI is 3.28% (house deck), so the run-rate is reproduced, not assumed. The fade to 6.1% by FY2030E comes only from the arithmetic of a fixed 800-store programme on a larger base (3.8% of the estate in 2026, 3.1% by FY2030E) plus CPI; no sourced constraint caps additions. Long run 5.5% = CPI plus a mature real increment, inside the house terminal cap.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: FY2025 21.90% and 9M2026 21.92% (S4, S3) — the format's margin has been flat for two years and the two chains compete on promotion, which caps expansion. Held at 21.92%, the 9M2026 actual, for FY2026E and every forecast year: no sourced basis for either expansion or compression, so the last actual is the most likely level.

assumptions.label: SG&A and other opex, net of recurring other income / revenue
assumptions.basis: Net opex ratio = (selling and distribution + G&A + other expenses - other income) / revenue: FY2025 18.30% (S4, notes 19/20/21a), 9M2025 18.36%, 9M2026 18.77% (S3). Held at 18.61% = 9M2026 actual blended with Q4's seasonal opex ratio; the 9M2026 wage-driven creep is a risk, not a base-case assumption.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 D&A 4,501.3 / revenue 126,737 = 3.55%, of which right-of-use depreciation 2,492.1 and fixed-asset depreciation 1,786.3 (S4 note 19). Held at 3.52% as the lease book grows with the store count.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 capex 4,994.7 (fixed assets 2,555.3 + right-of-use 2,297.7 + intangibles 141.7, S4 p.20) = 3.94% of revenue; the store programme needs roughly that to add ~800 outlets a year. Held at 3.95%.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Negative working capital: FY2025 nwc -2,244.1 on revenue 126,737 = -1.77%; 30 Sep 2026 nwc -2,389.2 on LTM revenue 133,549 = -1.79% (S0). Held at -1.78% — suppliers fund the shelf.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Set to reproduce the charge the LK actually carries, not the marginal rate: total finance cost of 127.163 in the nine months to 30 September 2026 annualises to about 169.6, which on opening borrowings of 2,710.4 is 6.26% (S3 p.7, note 22b). That charge covers bank-loan interest and lease interest together, so the rate is a calibrator on the borrowings-only debt line, not a market price for new debt. FY2025's effective rate was 7.33% (137.3 on opening debt 1,873.6, S4); the fall reflects refinancing of short-term bank lines. The 9.45% marginal rate is the WACC input only and is not charged to a company holding more cash than debt.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: FY2025 finance income 147.9 on opening cash 4,895.2 = 3.02% (S4).

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: No funded expansion plan: the company states capex is met from internal cash flow complemented by long-term bank debt only when needed (S6). Held at zero.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: 9M2026 actual: share of associates' loss 18.230 plus final tax 42.834 = -61.064, annualising to about -81 (S3 p.7). FY2025 was -187.6 (associates' loss 133.9 plus final tax 53.7, S4), but that level was driven by the Philippines associate's losses, which have narrowed to 18.2 over nine months as the carrying value fell to 348.7. Held at the observed run rate of -81 in every year: no source supports a return to the FY2025 level or a further improvement, and the item is small enough that a trend assumption would be invention.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: FY2025 minority 147.9 / net profit 3,558.8 = 4.2%; 9M2026 156.1 / 2,558.9 = 6.1% (S3) as the subsidiary formats (MIDI, LWS, SIL) grow faster than the parent banner and the LWS stake was diluted to 70% in May 2025 (S4 note). Held at the latest actual 6.1% rather than fading back to the FY2025 average.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Policy is a minimum, not a cap: 15-25% below IDR 250bn of profit and >25% above it (S6). FY2024 paid 44.99% and FY2025 paid 41.5/share = ~50% of EPS; an interim of 14.5/share was paid in October 2026, so the company now distributes twice a year. Held at 50%.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Treasury shares rose from 146.161m at 31 December 2025 to 432.669m at 30 September 2026, IDR532.835bn of purchases in the nine months (S3 p.6, p.9), leaving 41,091.8327m shares outstanding against the data pack's 41,378.3404m. FY2026E therefore carries -0.69% to the observed 30 September count. The buyback announced on 5 December 2025 ran to 6 March 2026 with a ceiling of IDR1.5trn or 650m shares (S3 p.110); no renewal is disclosed, so no further purchases are modelled from FY2027E.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 5.0% = the house terminal cap for rupiah names: CPI (house macro 3.28%) plus a real increment from a mature 24,000-store network, still below Indonesia's long-run nominal GDP (5.29% real + 3.28% CPI) and below the 6.1% FY2030E forecast. A network of this size cannot compound at nominal GDP for ever, but there is no sourced evidence it stops growing with the population.

challenges.challenge: Sections 2 and 5 assert that 'the trade ministry later suggested minimarkets could supply the cooperatives instead' and that cooperative stores are 'positioned as customers of the chains', both citing [S7]. S7 (4,689 chars) contains no reference to the trade ministry, to supply, or to cooperatives as customers: its only supply-related content is the Minister of Villages stopping new permits. No other archived source supports it (S2's sole 'memasok' is garlic seed). The claim is what turns the state from a competitor into a distributor and so props up the variant view on the single risk the report calls most damaging.
challenges.answer: Both sentences are cut. Section 2 now states only what S7 supports: the Minister of Villages stopped new permits rather than closures, the state is strengthening Kopdes Merah Putih, and the report frames the chains as unbalanced competition for local business [S7]. Section 5's cooperative risk is re-tested on that basis - a subsidised rural competitor rather than a distributor. The variant view no longer leans on a state-as-customer reading; it rests on licensing sitting with regencies and the minister's retreat from closure [S7][S11]. The "trade ministry" references in the signposts and section 7 are removed.

challenges.challenge: The update's core verification uses the wrong profit line. S12 reports laba bersih Rp2.4trn, +3.79% yoy, which is the LK's profit attributable to parent of 2,402.777 (S3 p.8, +3.79% on 2,314.904). The summary compares it with F18 = 2,558.885, total profit including minorities (+5.70% on 2,420.885), and calls them the same figure. The analyst's own fact labels contradict the text: F18's label says 'attributable to parent 2,402.777' and F33's says 'matches LK profit attributable to parent of 2,402.8'.
challenges.answer: The summary and section 3 now use the attributable line: F34 = 2,402.777, +3.79% on 2,314.904 (S3 p.8), which is what S12's Rp2.4trn and +3.79% refer to. F18 (2,558.885, +5.70%) is now labelled explicitly as total profit including minorities, in both the text and the fact label. The text also states that attributable profit grew at roughly half the 7.9% operating rate.

challenges.challenge: S12's one genuinely new piece of analysis is a comparison the report drops: AMRT net profit +3.79% against MIDI +19.44%, which the article attributes to margin and operational efficiency. MIDI is a covered peer in the same group and the stated driver is the Lawson ready-to-eat and ready-to-drink mix, i.e. a format question for Alfamart. The report instead says the item carries 'no new operating fact', so the only bearish signal in the trigger document is never weighed.
challenges.answer: Added in the summary and in section 2: MIDI nine-month net profit +19.44% against AMRT +3.79% (F41, F42), with the article's stated driver, the Lawson ready-to-eat/ready-to-drink mix. The report now says why it is consistent with holding gross margin at 21.92% - Alfamart's grocery mix is funded by supplier terms and we capitalise no margin expansion - and carries it in the bear case as a mix/efficiency risk: a format that cannot add fresh-food margin competes on price and location, which is the bear's 100bp gross-margin path. It also explains the below-EBIT dilution in section 3.

challenges.challenge: The base case has FY2026E attributable profit DOWN 6.6% to 3,186.1 from 3,410.9 while the nine months are already +3.8% and revenue +7.2%. Two lines produce it without source: interest expense rises 87% from 137.3 to 256.1 because the 9.45% WACC cost of debt is applied to the full 2,710.6 legacy balance on a net-cash company, and other_nonop is held at -200 against a nine-month actual of -61 (about -81 annualised). On the LK effective rate (about 7.3%) and the run-rate other_nonop, parent profit is about 3,320 - still below FY2025, which the report never discloses.
challenges.answer: Both inputs corrected. cost_of_debt 9.45% -> 6.26%: the LK's nine-month finance cost of 127.163 annualises to about 169.6 on opening borrowings of 2,710.4 (S3 p.7), so the rate reproduces the charge the company pays, including lease interest, instead of charging the marginal WACC rate to a net-cash balance sheet. other_nonop -200 -> -81: 9M2026 associates' loss 18.230 plus final tax 42.834 annualised (S3 p.7), against FY2025's -187.6. FY2026E attributable profit is now 3,342.7 (-2.0% on 3,410.9), EPS 81.3 against 82.4, and section 3 discloses that path with the nine-month EPS of 58.43 and the cause - 9M opex creep and a 6.1% minority take against about 4% in FY2025 (S3).

challenges.challenge: The company bought back IDR532.8bn of shares in 9M2026 (432.669m treasury shares at 30 Sep 2026 against 146.161m at FY2025, S3 p.6 and p.9), yet the capital-allocation paragraph omits it and assumptions.share_change still reads 'No rights issue, buyback or script dividend announced; 41,378m shares net of 146m treasury (S4)' while the model itself uses 41,091.8m shares. This is QC Q2 from 9 November, still unfixed.
challenges.answer: Basis corrected and the buyback stated. New facts: IDR532.835bn of treasury purchases in 9M2026 (S3 p.9) and 432.669m treasury shares against 146.161m at FY2025 (S3 p.6). share_change FY2026E is now -0.69%, rolling the share count to the observed 41,091.8m. One correction to the challenge: the engine's share line was 41,378.3m (the pack's FY2025A count), not 41,091.8m; the 41,091.8m figure is the 30 September actual, which the roll now reaches, closing a 0.7% overstatement. Section 3 states the buyback in the capital-allocation and payout discussion and says no further purchases are modelled because the disclosed programme expired in March 2026 with no renewal on file (S3 p.110).

challenges.challenge: Sections 3 and 5 say the trade receivables book is 'owed by related parties, franchise partners and suppliers' and that 'the notes give no related-party percentage'. S4 p.14 splits trade receivables: related parties IDR12.9bn against third parties IDR3,201.4bn, 0.4% of the book, and note 23 quantifies the related-party flows. Section 5's 'the rest owed by related parties' is therefore false, and it converts a 0.4% exposure into a named risk channel. This is QC Q1, still unfixed.
challenges.answer: The related-party framing is dropped. Sections 3, 5 and 6 now state the split the notes give: related parties IDR12.866bn against a IDR3,214.313bn trade book, 0.4%, with 53.6% current (S4 p.79 note 5). The "notes give no related-party percentage" sentence is deleted. The aging point, which was correctly sourced, is kept.

challenges.challenge: Section 4 says 'The DCF gives enterprise value of IDR58,382.4bn and Rp1,351 per share'. EV 58,382.4 is the dcf_fcff output, whose per-share value is Rp1,433.5; Rp1,351 is the 90/10 blend with the no-terminal-value leg (Rp613.5). The same paragraph compares a 4.2x entry EV/EBITDA that excludes the IDR1,406.7bn minority with a 5.7x exit multiple that is gross of it; on the bridge-consistent basis the entry is 4.3x. This is QC Q3, flagged and signed off as fixed on 9 November, and the text is unchanged.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now separates the two: the DCF is EV 58,382.4 and Rp1,433 a share; the 90/10 blend of that with the no-terminal-value leg at Rp614 is the base value of Rp1,351. On the multiple, one correction: the engine's 4.2x is already market capitalisation net of treasury shares plus net debt plus minority minus investments (the mcap/EV builder in cov_engine), so it is gross of the IDR1,406.7bn minority and the text now states that definition and applies it to both entry and implied exit, which is struck from the terminal value and is therefore also gross.

challenges.challenge: The BUY does not survive the bear scenario's probability being doubled. At 40% base and 60% bear the probability-weighted target is 0.4 x 1,468.3 + 0.6 x 545.6 = Rp915, 6% below the Rp975 price and roughly 20% below the cost of equity, and the bull's 25% probability supplies 46% of the Rp1,532 target. The report stress-tests WACC and terminal growth but never its own 45/30/25 weights, and gives no basis for 30% bear against a CAUTIOUS macro stance and an AVOID on rate-sensitive Indonesian consumer.
challenges.answer: Section 5 now tests its own weights. Holding the scenario values fixed, double the bear weight to 0.60, drop the bull and let the base carry 0.40: 0.4 x 1,466 + 0.6 x 544 = about 913, below the 975 price, and the report says so. It also states that the 25% bull supplies close to half the Rp1,530 target. The 30% bear stands on a sourced argument: it needs a demand recession and a national permit cap together, licensing sits with regencies and the minister has retreated from closure (S7, S11); 25% bull needs rules settled and purchasing power recovered in the same window. The house CAUTIOUS/AVOID stance applies to leveraged rate-sensitive consumer names; AMRT is net cash and rupiah-funded (S8), which is why it does not shift these weights. A second regency enforcing closures at scale is named as what would raise the bear weight.

challenges.challenge: Section 5 quotes the bear as 'Rp506' and the bull as 'Rp2,591', which are the pre-roll intrinsic values, while the scenario table and the Rp1,532 target weight the rolled values Rp545.6 and Rp2,829.9. A reader cannot reconcile the two sets. This is QC Q4, raised by the judge at 0.94 confidence on 9 November and still unlabelled. Separately, section 3's 'The trailing Rp56 is that final plus the October interim' no longer reconciles after the trim removed the 'FY2025 distribution' label: the FY2024 final of 34.11 plus the 14.5 interim is 48.6, not 56; it is 41.5 plus 14.5.
challenges.answer: Section 5 now quotes the rolled twelve-month values that the table and target weight (bear Rp544, base Rp1,466, bull Rp2,828) and labels the pre-roll intrinsic values (Rp506, Rp1,351, Rp2,591) explicitly as such; the thesis uses the rolled bear. The dividend line is restored to the FY2025 distribution: Rp41.50 per share approved on 4 June 2026 (F40, S3 p.110) plus the October interim, which reconciles to the trailing Rp56; the FY2024 final of Rp34.11 is no longer used as the base.

challenges.challenge: Investment summary still opens 'No change to the model ... change nothing in the forecast' although this revision moved FY2026E np_parent from 3,186.1 to 3,342.7, interest expense 256.1 to 169.7, other_nonop -200 to -81 and added a -0.69% share change.
challenges.answer: Opening now scopes the no-change claim to the 10 November S12 item and states the revised FY2026E attributable profit after restating finance cost and other non-operating items and carrying the treasury count.

challenges.challenge: assumptions qc_justifications extreme_call still carries pre-fix figures (+57% expected return, 12.7x FY2026E P/E, 17.5x at the 1,351 base) against model outputs 61.1% total return, 12.0x and 16.6x; this is the text that discharges the BLOCK flag.
challenges.answer: extreme_call justification refreshed to the engine outputs: 61.1% total return, 12.0x FY2026E earnings at 975, 16.6x at the 1,351 base, 17.6x DCF and 6.1x EV/EBITDA.

challenges.challenge: valuation post_bs_review still records net profit 2.56tn +5.37% - the total-profit line, where attributable profit is 2,402.777 +3.79% - and omits the IDR532.835bn buyback completed 6 March 2026 that the model's share_change reflects.
challenges.answer: post_bs_review now quotes attributable profit 2,402.777bn +3.79% [S3 p.8] and lists the IDR532.835bn treasury purchase that took treasury shares to 432.669m, 0.69% of the base.

missing_bull_case.note: The 9M2026 buyback is neither credited nor modelled: S3 p.6/p.9 show 432.669m treasury shares at 30 Sep 2026 against 146.161m at FY2025 and IDR532.8bn of purchases. The 'higher payout is the cheapest way to close the gap' lever is asserted, never sized. Credit: the reverse DCF (2.33% implied FY2027E growth) is now the core upside and the Philippines is bridged at IDR348.7bn.

missing_bear_case.note: The trigger's only comparative fact is omitted: S12 says AMRT net profit grew 3.79% while MIDI grew 19.44%, attributing the gap to margin and operating efficiency. A report that asserts 'no new operating fact' should say why its sibling beat it five-fold. Credit: the demand/recession bear, the receivable and minority channels and the value-trap section are now present and fairly argued.

assumption_realism.note: Revenue 7.2%, gross margin 21.92%, opex 18.61%, D&A 3.52%, capex 3.95% and tax 18.85% all tie to the LK, and 18.61% is arithmetically Q4-2025's 18.1% ratio rather than a haircut. But the FY2026E P&L is not the most likely path: attributable profit falls 6.6% to 3,186.1 on interest expense rising 137.3 to 256.1 with a flat debt balance and other_nonop held at -200 against a -61 nine-month actual.

evidence_and_citations.note: Verified: S12 revenue +7.21% and profit +3.79%; S7 minister stopping new permits only; S11 Perda 2021 one-kilometre rule and 25 outlets; S3 treasury IDR532.8bn; S4 related parties IDR12.9bn. Three fail: the trade-ministry 'supply the cooperatives' claim is in no archived source; 2,558.9 (total profit) is presented as the article's 2,400 (attributable 2,402.8); 'the notes give no related-party percentage' is false. 'Medicines now allowed' rests only on a KBLI classification.

valuation_method_fit.note: WACC 11.3% inside the IDR 11-13% band, TV 57.7% disclosed, implied exit 5.7x against 4.2x entry now stated honestly, reinvestment and ROIIC fade stated, multiple-survival test no longer backwards (credit). But section 4 pairs EV 58,382.4 with Rp1,351 per share when the DCF is Rp1,433 (1,351 is the 90/10 blend), and the 4.2x entry excludes minorities while the 5.7x exit is gross of them.

bias_and_tone.note: The report now says roughly four fifths of the 61.1% is re-rating and labels the value trap, which is honest. But it never tests its own weights: at 40% base and 60% bear the target is Rp915, below the price, and the 25% bull supplies 46% of the target; section 4's 'growth of 8.0%' is FY2027E while FY2026E EPS falls 6.6%; 'about a third higher' is 38.6%.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: CPI 3.28%, GDP 5.29%, usd/idr 18,350 and the CAUTIOUS balance-of-payments plus AVOID rate-sensitive consumer stances are all engaged in section 5. Beta 0.73, ERP 4.23%, CRP 2.46%, COE 11.5% and WACC 11.3% sit inside the house IDR 11-13% band; the 90/10 weights depart from the 60/30/10 STAPLES_RETAIL default with a sourced explanation; terminal g 5.0% is the house cap and below nominal GDP.

conservatism_audit.note: Downward without a source: interest expense up 87% (9.45% marginal rate on 2,710.6 of legacy debt), other_nonop -200 against an -81 run-rate, a 10% weight on a no-terminal-value leg that assumes the business ends in 2035, and share_change 0% against a 0.7% nine-month buyback. Upward: opex 18.61% is real Q4 arithmetic, not optimism. The base case brands itself most likely while carrying three unexplained downward drifts.

calibration.note: The ebitda_margin gate passes at -0.32pp (model 6.83% against 7.15%) and the FY2025A lines tie to S4. But calibration at the earnings line fails: FY2026E attributable profit is 6.6% below FY2025A while the nine months are 3.8% above it, and section 3 still does not state the Q4 opex ratio (18.1%) that makes the -32bp gap auditable (QC Q5). Both BLOCK and WARN flags are answered.

signoff.notes: Second sign-off. Round-1 returns closed: summary scopes the no-change claim and states the restated FY2026E profit; extreme_call refreshed to the engine outputs (61.1% total return, 12.0x, 16.6x at the base, 4.2x EV/EBITDA entry); post_bs_review quotes attributable profit 2,402.777 +3.79% and the buyback; 3,497 words, lint clean, facts PASS. Call judged sound: BUY 1,530 on 975 reproduces from weights 0.30/0.45/0.25 on 543.5/1,466.2/2,828.0 = 1,529.8; the base alone at 1,466 is +50%, so the call does not need the 25% bull; the bear 544 is on mirrored shocks to the same four drivers. The base case is the most likely path, not the cautious one: growth 7.2% is the 9M actual and the 800-store plan, gross margin is held at the 9M actual 21.92%, opex 18.61% blends the 9M 18.77% with Q4 seasonality rather than extrapolating a haircut, and the FY2026E profit dip is explained by that opex ratio and minority 6.1% vs 4.2% on LK actuals. Multiple-survival is run and disclosed (4.2x entry, 5.7x implied exit, about four fifths of the return is re-rating), the de-rating base rate and value trap are carried, and the reverse DCF solves to 2.3% growth. Compounder lens present: reinvestment about an eighth of NOPAT, ROIIC about 4x WACC, ROE fade 19.8% to 15.0%, terminal g 5.0% at the house cap, exit vs entry stated. Open FIX items do not change the call and are for the next update rather than another return: Q7 cites S9 for the Rp14.5 interim dividend where S3 carries it (Rp595.832, Rp14.50) and the 5 Dec 2025 to 6 Mar 2026 buyback dates are in S3 too, so re-cite S3; Q8 6.1x should read 6.3x EV/EBITDA (58,382.4 / 9,279.4) on enterprise value. Cross-name note: the bridge deducts minorities at book 1,406.7 while our MIDI mark implies about 1,899, so AMRT is understated by roughly Rp12 a share - conservative, not a defect.

bias.note: FY2026E reproduces the last actual's economics: 7.2% revenue is the 9M2026 actual (S3), gross margin held at the 9M2026 21.92% (S3/S4), and the only cautious departure, opex 18.30%->18.61%, is the 9M2026 actual ratio 18.77% blended with Q4 seasonality (S3), not a default haircut. The one favourable line, other_nonop -81 vs FY2025's -187.6, is sourced to the Philippines associate loss narrowing to 18.2 over nine months (S3). Scenarios mirror four drivers (+/-3pp revenue, +/-1pp GM, -/+0.5pp opex, +/-1pp terminal g) with base 45% >= bear 30%, and the target reproduces: 0.45x1,466.2 + 0.30x543.5 + 0.25x2,827.6 = 1,529.7.

findings.finding: post_bs_review, the payout basis and s6 attribute the IDR14.5/share (IDR595.83bn) interim dividend announced 5-6 Oct 2026 to [S9]; S9 (3,663 chars) contains no dividend reference and no archived AMRT source carries it, so the claim is true but untraced. The same block's buyback programme dates (5 December 2025 programme, expiry 6 March 2026) also appear in no archived source.

The extreme_call justification says the DCF 'values the equity at 17.6x and 6.1x EV/EBITDA'. 17.6x checks (1,433.5 / 81.35) and 5.7x checks (TV 89,602 / FY2035E EBITDA 15,631), but the DCF EV of 58,382.4 over FY2026E EBITDA of 9,279.4 is 6.3x, not 6.1x, and it is an enterprise- not equity-value multiple.

Finance cost is calibrated on opening gross debt of 2,710.4 while the 30 Sep 2026 accounts show lease-only debt of 1,985.4 with bank loans repaid (S3 p.5); FY2026E interest of 169.7 is about 45bn high. Immaterial to value; the judge raised the same NOTE.

s3 says 'Cash is accumulating ... IDR5,438.5bn against IDR2,710.4bn of debt', which are FY2025 year-end figures (S4); the report's latest balance sheet is 30 Sep 2026, where cash is 3,565.4 and debt 1,985.4 (S3). The undated comparison invites a stale read against the September net cash.

The cost-of-capital prose reads as beta x ERP (0.73 x 4.2%) plus CRP 2.5%, which builds to about 12.2%; the engine's 11.5% applies the CRP inside the beta (0.727 x 6.69%). s3's '18.6% against IDR23,193.9bn of cost on IDR126,737.3bn of revenue' also recomputes to 18.3%.

The dividend line shows FY2025A dps of 56.0, while the FY2025 dividend actually paid was IDR41.5/share (F40, S3). It is unused in the valuation (dps12 is FY2026E 40.67) but misstates the historical payout row.

flags.message: expected return +61%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: The 61.1% total return is a value-gap closure, not a cash-flow forecast, and we say so in section 4. At the 975 price the shares are 12.0x FY2026E earnings and 4.2x EV/EBITDA on one definition throughout — market capitalisation net of treasury shares plus net debt plus minority interest — after the MSCI Global Standard deletion and the permit rhetoric [S8][S7], while 9M2026 revenue grew 7.21%, operating profit 7.9% and attributable profit 3.79% [S3]. The DCF at an 11.3% WACC and 5.0% terminal growth values the equity at 17.6x and 6.1x EV/EBITDA, the blended base value of 1,351 capitalises FY2026E earnings at 16.6x, and the implied exit EV/EBITDA is 5.7x against the 4.2x entry on the same gross-of-minority basis, so roughly four fifths of the expected return is a re-rating; the cash-flow part (4.2% yield plus 7.7% FY2027E earnings growth) is roughly the 11.5% cost of equity, and FY2026E is the dip year in the accounts. Today's price implies FY2027E revenue growth of 2.33% against our 7.0% [S3].

flags.message: method weights differ from the industry default {'dcf_fcff': 0.6, 'pe': 0.3, 'ev_ebitda': 0.1}
flags.justification: DCF 90% / no-terminal-value DCF 10%, against the 60/30/10 industry default, because the only multiple benchmarks available are unusable: the own-history averages of 34x PE and 16x EV/EBITDA are the premium era the shares have given back, and the declared peer set has one modelled datapack (MIDI), below the three needed for a median [S0][S8]. Giving them weight would put the bubble or a single name into the target; the no-terminal-value case is the honest second anchor.
